followUps:
A zero gradient means you are at a flat spot, which is not always a minimum: it can be a minimum, a maximum or a saddle point. Gradient descent stops moving there because the step is lr times zero.

Example: f(x) = x2 has gradient 2x, zero at x = 0 (a minimum). f(x) = x3 has gradient 3x2, also zero at x = 0, yet it is neither a minimum nor a maximum. To tell them apart you look at curvature (the second derivative or Hessian). In practice, with noisy minibatches, an exactly zero gradient almost never happens; a tiny gradient norm with a flat loss curve is the sign to watch.

Because there is one partial derivative per parameter, so the gradient has exactly one number for every weight, in the same layout. That is what makes the update w = w - lr * g possible: you subtract element by element.

Example: a weight matrix W of shape 3x4 has 12 weights, so dL/dW is also 3x4, and entry (1,2) says how much the loss changes if only W[1][2] moves a little. A bias vector of length 4 gets a gradient of length 4. If a gradient you computed has a different shape than its parameter, you have made a mistake (often a missing transpose or a missing sum over the batch).

Because a network has millions of inputs (weights) but only one output (the scalar loss), and reverse mode gets all the input gradients in one backward sweep, while forward mode needs one sweep per input.

Example: with 1,000,000 weights, forward mode would need about 1,000,000 passes to fill the gradient; reverse mode needs one forward plus one backward pass, roughly 3x the cost of the forward alone. Forward mode wins only in the opposite case: few inputs and many outputs. The price of reverse mode is memory, since it must store the forward activations.

Because a parameter can feed into the loss through more than one path, and the true gradient is the sum of all those contributions; accumulating with += does that sum for you. It also lets you split a big batch into several micro-batches.

Example: you want an effective batch of 64 but memory only fits 16. Run 4 micro-batches, calling backward() on each (loss divided by 4), and the .grad buffers add up to the gradient of the full batch. Then call optimizer.step() once. The consequence is that you must call zero_grad() every step, or old gradients leak into the new one.

code.title: Learning rate on f(x) = 2(x-3)^2: converge, crawl, diverge
code.python:
a, c = 2.0, 3.0          # f(x) = a*(x-c)^2, minimum at x = c
print("f(x) = 2(x-3)^2, start x=0, 10 steps")
for lr in (0.01, 0.2, 0.6):
    x = 0.0
    for step in range(10):
        grad = 2 * a * (x - c)      # df/dx
        x -= lr * grad              # error is multiplied by (1 - 2*a*lr)
    factor = 1 - 2 * a * lr
    print(f"lr={lr:.2f} factor={factor:.2f} x={x:.4f}")
# converges only when |factor| < 1, i.e. lr < 1/a = 0.5

followUps:
A learning-rate finder is a short test run where the learning rate is increased steadily (for example from 1e-7 to 1) while you record the loss, to find a good range quickly.

Steps: start tiny, multiply the rate by a constant factor each batch, plot loss against rate on a log axis, and stop when the loss blows up. Pick a value a bit below where the loss starts to explode, typically about one order of magnitude lower than the minimum of the curve, where the loss is still falling steeply. It costs only a few hundred steps, and it gives a starting point for the schedule, not the final answer.

A common rule of thumb is to scale the learning rate with the batch size: double the batch, increase lr by about 2x (linear scaling, used with SGD) or by about 1.4x (square-root scaling, often used with Adam). It is a starting point, not a law.

Reason: a bigger batch gives a less noisy gradient, so you can afford a larger step, and you also take half as many steps per epoch, so each step should do more. Example: lr 0.1 at batch 256 becomes 0.2 at batch 512. Very large batches need a longer warm-up, and the rule stops working beyond a critical batch size, so check the loss curve.

code.title: Gradient on the logit: MSE through sigmoid vs cross-entropy
code.python:
import math

y = 1.0                              # the true label is 1
print("true label y=1; gradient of the loss w.r.t. the logit z")
for z in (-4.6, 0.0, 4.6):
    p = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z))       # sigmoid output
    mse = 2 * (p - y) * p * (1 - p)  # (p-y)^2 through sigmoid: extra p(1-p) factor
    ce = p - y                       # cross-entropy: just p - y
    print(f"z={z:.1f} p={p:.4f} mse_grad={mse:.4f} ce_grad={ce:.4f}")
# confidently wrong (z=-4.6): MSE gradient is tiny, so learning stalls

followUps:
Perplexity is the exponential of the average cross-entropy loss (in nats): perplexity = eloss. Read it as the number of equally likely choices the model is effectively hesitating between at each step.

Example: if every token gets probability 0.25, the loss is ln 4 = 1.386 and perplexity is 4. A model that guesses uniformly over a 50,000-word vocabulary has perplexity 50,000; a good language model on its own domain may reach 10 to 30. Lower is better, but only compare models that use the same tokenizer and the same test text.

About ln 10, which is 2.303, because a model that has learned nothing yet should spread its probability evenly: each class gets 0.1, and -ln 0.1 = 2.303.

This is a quick sanity check before training. If the first loss is 2.3 you are on track; if it is 15, your initial outputs are too large or confident (bad initialisation or missing scaling); if it is 0 or NaN, something is broken. The general value is ln K for K balanced classes, for example ln 50000 = 10.8 for a language model with a 50,000-token vocabulary.

code.title: Softmax + cross-entropy gradient equals p - one_hot, checked numerically
code.python:
import math

z = [2.0, 1.0, 0.1]                  # logits
t = 0                                # target class

def loss(z):
    m = max(z)                       # log-sum-exp trick for stability
    lse = m + math.log(sum(math.exp(v - m) for v in z))
    return lse - z[t]                # L = -z_t + ln(sum e^z_j)

m = max(z)
e = [math.exp(v - m) for v in z]
p = [v / sum(e) for v in e]          # softmax probabilities
grad = [p[i] - (1.0 if i == t else 0.0) for i in range(3)]   # p - one_hot
print("p =", " ".join(f"{v:.4f}" for v in p))
eps = 1e-5
for i in range(3):
    zp = list(z); zp[i] += eps
    zm = list(z); zm[i] -= eps
    num = (loss(zp) - loss(zm)) / (2 * eps)    # central difference
    print(f"i={i} analytic={grad[i]:.4f} numeric={num:.4f}")
print(f"sum of gradient = {abs(sum(grad)):.4f}")

followUps:
Label smoothing replaces the hard target (1 for the true class, 0 elsewhere) with a softer one, so the gradient is still p - target but the target is no longer exactly one-hot.

With K classes and smoothing e, the true class gets 1 - e + e/K and each other class gets e/K. Example: K = 3, e = 0.3 gives target [0.8, 0.1, 0.1]. The gradient on the logits is p - [0.8, 0.1, 0.1], so it reaches zero when p equals those values rather than when p = [1, 0, 0]. The logits no longer have to grow without bound, which reduces over-confidence and acts as a mild regulariser.

For numerical stability and speed. Computing softmax first and then taking log can overflow or underflow, while a fused operation works directly on the logits with the log-sum-exp trick.

Example: logits [1000, 0]. exp(1000) overflows to infinity, so the naive softmax gives NaN. The fused form computes L = -zt + m + ln(sum e^(z - m)) with m = max(z), where every exponent is at most 0, so it is safe. It also has the simple backward p - one_hot, so it needs no big Jacobian and saves memory and kernel launches. In PyTorch this is why you pass raw logits to CrossEntropyLoss.

With ReLU the activation slope is 1 where the pre-activation is positive and 0 where it is negative, so the backward rule becomes a mask instead of h(1 - h).

In the steps: delta1 = dh * (z1 > 0). Example: z1 = [2, -1, 0.5] and dh = [0.3, 0.7, -0.2] give delta1 = [0.3, 0, -0.2]. The unit with a negative input passes no gradient back (a dead unit for that example). Everything else is unchanged: dW1 = delta1 times x transposed, db1 = delta1. The mask is cheap and does not shrink gradients, which is one reason ReLU avoids the vanishing gradient problem of sigmoid.

Because the local derivative of most layers depends on the values that went through it in the forward pass, so those values must be kept or recomputed.

Examples: for a weight matrix, dW = delta times the layer input transposed, so you need the input x. For a sigmoid, the slope is h(1 - h), so you need the output h. For ReLU you need the sign of z. This is why training uses much more memory than inference: it stores the activations of every layer. Activation checkpointing trades compute for memory by storing only some layers and recomputing the rest during backward.

code.title: Gradient check: central differences catch a missing factor of 2
code.python:
import math

def f(w):                            # loss: w0^2 * w1 + sin(w1)
    return w[0] ** 2 * w[1] + math.sin(w[1])

def good(w):                         # correct analytic gradient
    return [2 * w[0] * w[1], w[0] ** 2 + math.cos(w[1])]

def buggy(w):                        # forgot the factor 2 in d/dw0
    return [w[0] * w[1], w[0] ** 2 + math.cos(w[1])]

def numeric(w, k, eps=1e-5):
    wp = list(w); wp[k] += eps
    wm = list(w); wm[k] -= eps
    return (f(wp) - f(wm)) / (2 * eps)       # central difference

w = [1.5, 0.5]
print("w =", w)
for name, fn in (("good", good), ("buggy", buggy)):
    g = fn(w)
    for k in range(2):
        n = numeric(w, k)
        rel = abs(g[k] - n) / (abs(g[k]) + abs(n))   # relative error
        status = "ok" if rel < 1e-6 else "BUG"
        print(f"{name} param {k}: analytic={g[k]:.5f} numeric={n:.5f} rel={rel:.4f} {status}")

followUps:
Because the error of a forward difference shrinks only in proportion to eps, while the error of a central difference shrinks in proportion to eps squared, so it is much more accurate for the same eps.

Example: f(x) = x3 at x = 1 (true slope 3), eps = 0.01. Forward: (1.0303 - 1) / 0.01 = 3.0301, error 0.03. Central: (1.030301 - 0.970299) / 0.02 = 3.0001, error 0.0001. The price is two function evaluations per parameter instead of one (one if you reuse f(x)), which is fine for a check run on a small model.

Test the backward on its own with small inputs, compare against an independent reference, and cover the awkward cases such as odd shapes and boundary values.

Steps: (1) run the kernel in float64 on tiny random inputs and compare its gradient to central differences of the forward kernel; (2) compare against a plain CPU or PyTorch implementation of the same function; (3) use non-square, non-multiple-of-block sizes to catch indexing errors; (4) run twice to check results are deterministic or within a tolerance; (5) for atomics, expect small float differences. PyTorch's gradcheck automates step 1.

Adam's two averages m and v are initialised at zero, so early on they are biased toward zero (too small); bias correction divides by 1 - beta^t to fix that.

Example: beta2 = 0.999, first gradient g = 1. Then v = 0.001 * 1 = 0.001, so sqrt(v) = 0.032 and the step would be about 31 times too big. Dividing by 1 - 0.999 = 0.001 gives v-hat = 1 and a step of about lr. The correction fades away as t grows (1 - 0.999^t approaches 1 after a few thousand steps), which is the same time warm-up is usually applied.

Two extra numbers per parameter (m and v), plus the parameter and its gradient. In 32-bit that is 8 extra bytes per parameter on top of the 4-byte weight and 4-byte gradient.

Example: a 7-billion-parameter model has 7e9 x 4 B = 28 GB of weights, 28 GB of gradients and 56 GB of Adam state, so about 112 GB before activations. SGD with momentum needs one buffer instead of two. This is why large runs shard the optimiser state (ZeRO/FSDP), use 8-bit optimisers, or keep the state in lower precision.

torch.optim.Adam(weight_decay=...) implements plain L2 regularisation: it adds weight_decay times w to the gradient before the Adam update. The decoupled version is a separate class, torch.optim.AdamW.

The difference matters because in Adam that added term gets divided by sqrt(v-hat), so weights with large gradients are barely decayed. With AdamW the decay is applied directly as w = w - lr * wd * w. Example: lr 1e-3 and wd 0.01 shrink every weight by a factor 1 - 1e-5 per step, regardless of the gradient. Use AdamW when you want true weight decay.

Because decay pushes values toward zero, and for biases and normalisation scales that is not helpful: a LayerNorm scale should usually sit near 1, and shrinking it just fights the model.

Also, these parameters are few (one number per feature), so they add little overfitting risk and do not need regularisation. Example: shrinking a LayerNorm gain from 1.0 toward 0 would dampen that whole feature at every layer. The usual recipe puts only weight matrices (2-D tensors) in the decay group and sets weight_decay = 0 for 1-D tensors such as biases and norm weights.

Gradient clipping limits the size of the gradient before the update, so one extreme batch cannot throw the weights far away. The common form clips by global norm.

Steps: compute the norm g = sqrt(sum of all squared gradient entries); if g exceeds the threshold c, multiply every gradient by c / g. Example: c = 1.0 and g = 8 give a scale of 0.125, so the direction stays the same and the length becomes 1. In PyTorch: torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, 1.0) after backward and before step. Logging the norm before clipping also tells you how often it triggers.

Because bf16 has the same exponent range as fp32 (about 1e-38 to 3e38), while fp16 tops out at 65,504 and underflows below about 6e-8. So bf16 rarely overflows or loses small gradients.

Example: a gradient of 1e-9 becomes 0 in fp16 (lost) but is kept in bf16; a logit sum of 70,000 overflows to infinity in fp16 and gives NaN. bf16 has fewer mantissa bits (about 3 decimal digits against 4 for fp16), so values are less precise, but that is usually fine for training. fp16 needs loss scaling to work around underflow; bf16 usually does not.

L1 gives sparse weights because its penalty has a constant pull toward zero (the gradient is lambda times the sign of w, whatever the size of w), while L2's pull gets weaker as w gets smaller.

Example: lambda = 0.1, w = 0.05. L1 subtracts a fixed amount each step (lr x 0.1), so w reaches exactly 0 in a few steps and stays there. L2 subtracts lr x 0.2 x w = proportional to 0.05, so w shrinks by a fixed fraction each step and only gets close to 0 without hitting it. Geometrically, the L1 constraint is a diamond with corners on the axes, where the solution tends to land.

At inference dropout is switched off, so every unit is used, and the outputs are scaled so their expected size matches what the network saw in training.

Modern implementations use inverted dropout: during training, with keep probability 0.8, surviving activations are divided by 0.8; at inference nothing changes. Example: an activation of 1.0 becomes 1.25 when kept and 0 when dropped (mean 1.0), and at inference it stays 1.0. Forgetting model.eval() leaves dropout on and makes predictions noisy and worse, a classic bug. (Keeping it on at inference is a deliberate trick called Monte Carlo dropout, used to estimate uncertainty.)

Look at the Hessian (matrix of second derivatives) at the point where the gradient is zero and check the signs of its eigenvalues.

All positive: a minimum. All negative: a maximum. Mixed signs: a saddle point, because the loss goes up in some directions and down in others. Example: f(x, y) = x2 - y2 has gradient zero at (0, 0) and Hessian diag(2, -2), a saddle: moving along x raises the loss, moving along y lowers it. For big networks the full Hessian is too large, so people estimate the top eigenvalues with Hessian-vector products instead.

Double descent is the surprising pattern where test error goes down, then up, then down again as model size (or training time) grows past the point where the model can just fit the training data exactly.

The classic U-shaped curve says bigger models overfit. But beyond the interpolation threshold, where parameters roughly equal the number of training points and the error peaks, even larger models often generalise better again, since among many perfect fits, training tends to find smooth ones. The practical lesson: do not stop growing a model just because validation error rose once, and be careful with early stopping around that peak.

Save the optimiser state and the step counter with the model, then rebuild the scheduler so its learning rate is a function of the global step, not of how many times the process started.

Steps: checkpoint model weights, optimiser state (Adam's m and v) and step; on resume, load all three and compute lr = schedule(step). Example: with 1,000 warm-up steps and a cosine decay, resuming at step 6,200 must give the lr for step 6,200, not restart the warm-up at 0. Also restore the random seed or data-loader position if you want identical data order. Resetting Adam's state causes a brief loss bump.

The schedule becomes far too coarse: warm-up and decay happen in huge jumps, and the learning rate is wrong for most of training.

Example: a 3-epoch run with 10,000 steps per epoch and a warm-up configured as 1,000 steps. Stepping per epoch would count only 3 steps in total, so warm-up would last the whole run (lr stuck at about 3/1000 of the target), or a cosine decay would hit its end after 3 epochs in 3 big jumps. Call scheduler.step() once per optimiser step, unless the scheduler was explicitly defined in epochs.

Because a model that cannot memorise a handful of examples certainly cannot learn the full dataset, so failing here reveals a bug in code, not a data or tuning problem.

Steps: take one batch (say 8 examples), turn off dropout and augmentation, train for 100 to 300 steps and expect the loss to drop to nearly 0. If it stalls, suspect the loss function, labels, learning rate, a detached tensor or a missing optimizer.step(). Example: stuck at loss 2.3 for 10 classes means the model is not learning at all (it is still at ln 10). It takes a minute and rules out the most common errors before spending GPU hours.

Assert the properties that must always hold, as cheap checks that fail loudly: shapes, finite values, and that something actually changed.

Examples: the loss is finite and the gradient norm is finite; every trainable parameter has a gradient that is not None; parameters change after step() (compare a checksum before and after); the learning rate at step 0 equals the expected warm-up start; the model is in train mode for training and eval mode for validation; label and logit shapes agree; the padding mask removes padding tokens from the loss; and the initial loss is close to ln K.
